profile.summary: DeepProt-T5 is a set of protein property predictors made by the DeepProtein authors. They took Prot-T5-XL, an existing protein language model, and fine-tuned it separately on each task of their benchmark, so there is one checkpoint per task rather than a single general model. Each checkpoint takes a protein sequence and returns the prediction for its task, for example a stability value, a subcellular location or a per-residue epitope label. The authors report it as the strongest entry in their own benchmark on several tasks.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DeepProt-T5 is not a new architecture. The DeepProtein authors took Prot-T5-XL, a 3B parameter protein language model from ProtTrans, and fine-tuned it separately on each of their benchmark datasets with the Hugging Face trainer. The difference from their other protein language model runs is that the upstream weights are updated during training rather than frozen, which they call dynamic rather than fixed embeddings. Each task therefore has its own checkpoint, and together they form the series the paper calls DeepProt-T5.

sections.title: Training setup the authors report
sections.body: For the DeepProt-T5 fine-tunes the paper gives a learning rate of 0.00002 for every model and a batch size of 10, chosen to avoid memory errors, against a default of 0.0001 and batch size 32 for the library's other sequence models. The maximum number of training epochs for all models is 100. The fine-tuning ran on two 24 GB NVIDIA RTX 3090 cards.

quotes.text: For DeepProt-T5 models, fine-tuning has used a more generalized learning rate of 0.00002 for all models, batch size is equal to 10 to avoid memory errors
For all models, the maximal training epoch number is set to 100.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There is one checkpoint per benchmark task rather than a single model. The paper and the README both say the fine-tuned models are released in the Hugging Face collection jiaxie/protlm. When that collection was read through the API on 2026-11-26 its item list was empty, so no individual checkpoint could be pinned to a revision, and the per-task parameter counts and sizes could not be read. A result should name the task, the seed (the paper uses 7, 42 and 100) and the library commit; the code is at github.com/jiaqingxie/DeepProtein, read here at commit 63247833.

sections.title: What the authors claim for it
sections.body: The abstract says the DeepProt-T5 series reaches the best reported performance on four of the benchmark tasks and is competitive on six others. In the results text the authors say their DeepProt-T5 models improved on the original Prot-T5 models on six tasks, named as Beta-lactamase, Solubility, SubCellular, PPI_Affinity, CRISPR and Fold. These are the authors' own claims about their own benchmark.

facts.label: Model type
facts.value: Task-specific fine-tunes of a protein language model, one checkpoint per benchmark task.

quotes.text: a series of fine-tuned Prot-T5-based models
We have released our fine-tuned Prot-T5-XL models for each task

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: Prot-T5-XL, which the paper describes as based on the T5-3B model with a BART-like masked language modelling objective and an embedding dimension of 1024, with the upstream weights updated during task fine-tuning.

quotes.text: Prot-T5-XL-UniRef50 is based on the T5-3B model
this model uses a BART-like MLM denoising objective
The embedding dimension is 1024.

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: A protein sequence as a string, or a pair of sequences for the interaction tasks. The paper says protein language models are given the initial string rather than a transformed representation.

quotes.text: we directly use the initial string as the input instead of the transformed SMILES

facts.label: Outputs
facts.value: The prediction for the task the checkpoint was fine-tuned on: a number for the regression tasks, a class for the classification tasks, and a per-residue label for the epitope and paratope tasks.

quotes.text: For the binary classification task, metrics are ROC (or PR-AUC) and averaged macro F1.
For multi classification task, metrics are the accuracy and averaged macro F1

facts.label: Parameters
facts.value: Not reported per checkpoint. The base model Prot-T5-XL is described as T5-3B, but the sources give no parameter count for the DeepProt-T5 fine-tunes and the released collection listed no items when read.

facts.label: Training data
facts.value: The DeepProtein benchmark datasets, one per checkpoint. The README lists them as Fluorescence, Solubility, Stability, Beta-lactamase, SubCellular, SubCellular-Binary, PPI_Affinity, Human_PPI, Yeast_PPI, Fold and Secondary Structure from PEER, plus IEDB, PDB-Jespersen, SAbDab-Liberis, TAP, SAbDab-Chen and CRISPR-Leenay from TDC. The underlying language model was pretrained on protein sequences before that.

quotes.text: | Fluorescence | PEER | LMDB | Protein Property Prediction |
| CRISPR-Leenay | TDC | TAB | CRISPR Repair Outcome Prediction  |

facts.label: Known versions
facts.value: One fine-tuned checkpoint per benchmark task, published as the ProtLM collection on Hugging Face. The collection's item list was empty when read on 2026-11-26, so the individual checkpoint names and revisions could not be recorded.

run_guide.summary: Install the DeepProtein environment, then run the library's one-line training command with the Prot-T5 encoder, which is the fine-tuning that produces a DeepProt-T5 checkpoint for a task.
prerequisites: Conda, and Python 3.9 as the README's environment line specifies.
Torch 2.1 or newer, which the README requires, with a matching CUDA build for GPU use.
A GPU with enough memory for fine-tuning a 3B parameter model. The authors used two 24 GB NVIDIA RTX 3090 cards for the DeepProt-T5 fine-tuning.
A weights and biases project name if the argument form of the command is used, since the README's examples pass wandb_proj.

steps.title: Create the environment and install the dependencies
steps.shell:
conda create -n DeepProtein python=3.9
conda activate DeepProtein
pip install git+https://github.com/bp-kelley/descriptastorus
pip install lmdb seaborn wandb pydantic DeepPurpose
pip install transformers bitsandbytes 
pip install accelerate>=0.26.0
pip install SentencePiece einops rdchiral peft
pip install numpy==1.23.5 pandas==1.5.3 scikit-learn==1.2.2
pip install datasets
conda install -c conda-forge pytdc
steps.explanation: The README installation block, copied as it stands.

quotes.text: python train/beta.py --target_encoding CNN --seed 7 --wandb_proj DeepProtein --lr 0.0001 --epochs 100

steps.title: Fine-tune Prot-T5 on one task
steps.explanation: This is the README's one-line training command for the Beta-lactamase task, with the encoder set to prot_t5, which the README's argument table lists as a supported protein encoder, and the learning rate set to the 0.00002 the paper reports for DeepProt-T5 fine-tuning. The README gives no command specific to DeepProt-T5, so the encoder and learning rate were put together from those two sources; the paper also reports a batch size of 10 for these fine-tunes, which this command does not set.
steps.source_locator: README: Example, Case Study 1(a) and argument table; paper: Training setup

outputs: A fine-tuned model for the chosen task, with training and test metrics. The README says results are logged to the weights and biases project named by wandb_proj, and the paper reports Spearman and Pearson correlation and mean absolute error for regression tasks.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository README at commit 6324783383cda5b46d635e3d9ac2dfdbf629ee0a and from the paper, and have not been executed by Rewire.
The sources give no command for downloading a released DeepProt-T5 checkpoint, because the collection listed no items when read, so this guide fine-tunes rather than loads.
The README's own notebook for inference with DeepProtT5 models is a Colab link and was not read.

notes: This is a real release, not a generic architecture, but the weights could not be verified: the paper and README both point at the Hugging Face collection jiaxie/protlm, and the API response for that collection listed no items on 2026-11-26, so no per-task checkpoint name, revision, parameter count or licence is recorded. A human should open the collection page in a browser to see whether items exist but are not served by the API. The fine-tuning command in the run guide is assembled from the README's argument table (prot_t5 as a target encoding) and the paper's learning rate, because the README gives no DeepProt-T5 specific command; the explanation says so. The record overlaps 11-prot-t5, which covers the base ProtT5 model from ProtTrans; they are separate models and the fine-tunes carry no licence of their own.
